title: Forecasting Daily Household Electricity Demand in a Hot-Arid City: A Comparative Benchmark of Local, Global, Deep and Foundation Models on ESHED-38

primary_sources.paraphrase: Single-author preprint (B. Neupane, stat.AP, v1, 2026-10-12). 24 configurations on ESHED-38 (38 homes in Erbil, daily, 2020-2025), 48 weekly origins over a 359-day test, leads to 30 days. Best configurations cut seasonal-naive scaled error by 20-25%; zero-shot Chronos-2 is significantly best at 1 day and tied at 1 week. Recorded weather improved no model; the weather record looks reused.

Full text. Test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17, Sunday origins, scored at h1, h7, h30 relative to seasonal naive: Chronos-2 gMASE 0.746 (h1) and 0.780 (h7); weather ensemble 0.797 (h30). Weather track uses recorded weather of the forecast days. Code is a notebook available on request; no pre-registration stated; no Chronos-2 revision given; no intervals on headline metrics.

ESHED-38 on Mendeley Data, version 2, by Jaf and Hamarash, published 2026-05-20, CC BY 4.0: daily kWh for 38 Erbil homes from ministry smart meters, 14 May 2020 to 17 June 2025, with a building survey and weather from sensors near the houses. Files were not inspected.
amazon/chronos-2 metadata: licence apache-2.0, created 2025-10-30, head 29ec3766 (2026-06-05), weights file model.safetensors.
Commit history of amazon/chronos-2: the commit titled as adding weights and config is 95a9710e on 2025-10-30; the ten other commits are README, tag or guide changes by title.

claims.text: The best of 24 configurations reduce the geometric-mean scaled error of a seasonal-naive forecast by 20 to 25%, and the leading models beat it in all 38 houses.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: Zero-shot Chronos-2 at one day ahead: relative gMASE 0.746 against seasonal naive, significantly ahead of all 23 other configurations.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: Zero-shot Chronos-2 at one day ahead: relative scaled CRPS 0.722 against seasonal naive.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: At one week, zero-shot Chronos-2 has relative gMASE 0.780, the same as TimesFM-2.5 and the pre-specified univariate ensemble; the three are statistically tied (adjusted p 0.51).
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: At 30 days the weather ensemble leads with relative gMASE 0.797, statistically tied with the univariate ensemble, TimesFM-2.5 and Chronos-2.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: At 30 days the weather ensemble has relative scaled CRPS 0.739 against seasonal naive.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: Giving a model the recorded weather of the forecast days improved none of the models run in both tracks, Chronos-2 included; the author attributes this to a weather record in which 68% of dates carry a temperature repeated on other dates and treats the value of weather as unresolved.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

claims.text: Deep networks trained from scratch (N-HiTS, PatchTST, TFT, DeepAR) do not beat per-house exponential smoothing on average.
claims.dataset: ESHED-38, 38 homes in Erbil, daily kWh, test 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17

relevance.rationale: Electric load, but daily energy of single households, not hourly zonal demand; the scale has no entry for non-hourly load, so 2 rather than 3 or 1 is a judgement, as on an earlier scorecard for daily national load. Weekly origins with a one-week bucket (h7) match a week-ahead issue cycle, at daily rather than hourly steps (3); 1-day and 30-day buckets are also reported. A weather track gives recorded weather of the forecast days as a known-future input, which corresponds to our oracle regime only, with no forecast regime (3); the paper itself doubts that weather record.

checks.notes: Central model: Chronos-2, zero-shot, the only model named in the headline claim. pre_registered: the paper states no registration; only the ensemble membership is said to be fixed before testing, with nothing public to date it. training_overlap_risk (about our run): the amazon/chronos-2 commit titled as adding the weights is dated 2025-10-30, before the first scored week (2025-11-10), so all 52 scored weeks start after it; the date is inferred from the commit title, per-commit files were not listed. independent_replication: three searches found no replication, re-run or code; the paper calls itself the first benchmark on this dataset. evidence_strength is moderate and that is a judgement: the data are public (CC BY 4.0), the test window is 359 days, the method uses named open libraries and the seasonal-naive baseline has the same inputs as the univariate models; it misses pre-registration and replication, and the code is only available from the author on request (the conclusion says the pipeline is released, which the availability statement contradicts). A stricter reading of 'numbers without code' would make it weak. baseline_same_inputs: yes for univariate Chronos-2 against seasonal naive; no for the weather ensemble against seasonal naive; partly for the 20-25% range, which spans univariate and weather configurations. Limits of the study: one city, one test year, 38 houses, a single author, no intervals on headline metrics (significance from rank tests with houses as pairs), a weather record the author suspects is a reused annual sequence (unconfirmed with the data owners), and recorded rather than forecast weather. In the study's own test, 2024-06-24 to 2025-06-17 lies before the Chronos-2 weights date; whether Chronos-2's training data could include this period was not checked (the dataset itself was published in May 2026). Unverified: all numbers were read through fetch summaries of the arXiv HTML in two chunks, no table was read directly; whether the 0.746 and 0.780 belong to the univariate or the weather run of Chronos-2 (taken as univariate, since weather improved no model); whether h7 means lead day 7 or days 1 to 7; which Chronos-2 revision and chronos-forecasting version were used (not stated); context length given to the foundation models; the Mendeley files were not opened; the TimesFM-2.5 and Chronos-Bolt weights dates were not checked.

label: ACCEPT_RUN
label_reason: A sourced benchmark on electric load with weekly origins and a one-week lead whose headline comparison, zero-shot Chronos-2 against seasonal naive, can be re-measured with models already in runnable_models, with weights dated before our scored window. The fit is partial and the evidence only moderate: daily household energy rather than hourly zonal load, code available only on request, no pre-registration, replication or intervals, and a weather record the author considers unreliable, so the weather finding is not usable as a claim.
implementation_hint: Central model amazon/chronos-2 (apache-2.0), direct_adapter via models/chronos2.py, weights commit 95a9710e (2025-10-30), 52 of 52 scored weeks after the weights. The headline maps to the existing univariate Chronos-2 row against seasonal_naive, a secondary comparison that needs no new run if both rows are on the leaderboard under the current protocol; the receipt must state the horizon mismatch (the study's one-week bucket of daily household energy against 168 hourly steps of zonal load) and that the study's baseline is seasonal naive, not the temperature-only regression. The no-gain-from-weather finding would correspond to Chronos-2 with and without temperature in the oracle regime only, but the study's weather record is doubted by its own author, so it should not be framed as a claim to transfer. Other models in the study: google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch (ff_univariate, models_ff/run_ff.py) tied at one week; Chronos-Bolt (FoundationForecast wrapper, ff_univariate); the two ensembles, AutoETS, AutoARIMA, ARIMAX, AutoTheta, LightGBM, XGBoost, N-HiTS, PatchTST, TFT and DeepAR are trained per dataset and are not rows we have.
